sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Hall County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Two Gainesville offices split the work. The Board of Assessors sets the value of every parcel, and the Hall County Tax Commissioner bills and collects the tax. Millage rates come from the County Commission, the Board of Education and each city that levies its own tax.

Hall County covers 429 square miles, 393 of them land, in the upper Piedmont just below the Blue Ridge foothills. The whole county makes up the Gainesville metro area, Gainesville is the county seat, and the Chattahoochee River gathers strength here on its way to Lake Sidney Lanier. The county was created in 1818, and the incorporated places are Gainesville, Buford, Flowery Branch, Oakwood, Lula, Gillsville, Braselton and Clermont. Most of the county sits in the Hall County School District, while parcels inside the city limits of Buford and Gainesville fall under those cities' own school systems, which changes the millage that applies.

  • Assessment questions: Board of Assessors, 2875 Browns Bridge Road, Gainesville, 770.531.6720 for real property.
  • Billing and payment questions: Tax Commissioner, 770.531.6950 option 3, open Monday through Friday 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • City bills: owners inside Gainesville, Flowery Branch, Buford, Braselton or Oakwood receive a second statement from that city.

sections.h2: When are Hall County property tax bills due?
sections.html:
Hall County bills are due 60 days after the mailing date. In a normal year they go out September 15 with a November 15 due date. The 2026 bills were mailed October 15 and fall due December 15, 2026, because the digest was approved late.

The county explains that the 60 day gap stays fixed even when the mailing slips, so a later bill gives you a later deadline. Unpaid balances start collecting interest each month after the due date. Read the due date printed on your own statement before you plan a payment, since the mailing date drives it.

Paying early is easy. The online portal at HallCountyTax.org shows payment status for every parcel and keeps records and receipts for the past ten years. Hall County lists E-Check as the cheapest route, at a flat $1.50. Credit cards carry a 2.49% fee and debit cards 1.50%. You can also mail the pay slip to P.O. Box 1579, Gainesville, GA 30503, use the 24 hour drop box under the breezeway at the Government Center on Browns Bridge Road, or pay by phone with a card.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Hall County assessment?
sections.html:
File within 45 days of the date printed on your assessment notice. Hall County accepts appeals online through qPublic, by mail to P.O. Box 2895, Gainesville, GA 30503, or in person at 2875 Browns Bridge Road.

If you do nothing in that window, the value goes to the Tax Commissioner for billing. The notices are mailed to every owner each year, and the 2026 digital copies were posted on qPublic.

An appeal does not pause the bill. Hall County sends an Under Appeal statement for the 2026 cycle, and the amount due by December 15, 2026 is the lower result of 85% of the 2026 value or 100% of the 2025 value. Any unpaid portion still accrues monthly interest from that date. Georgia's Department of Revenue notes that a refund after a final appeal decision is processed automatically, and that other refund claims for erroneous or illegal taxes must start within three years of payment.

sections.h2: What exemptions and filing deadlines apply in Hall County?
sections.html:
Filing season runs January 1 through April 1. Homestead applications, real property returns and personal property returns all use that window, and Hall County lets you do most of it online through qPublic.

  • Homestead exemptions, including the senior exemptions, the Total School Tax Exemption and the 100% Disabled Veteran exemption, are filed under the Real Property tab in qPublic.
  • Boats, personal watercraft, aircraft, business personal property and manufacturer personal property returns go under the Personal Property tab. Returns filed after April 1 carry a 10% late filing penalty.
  • Conservation Use covenants must be filed in person at the Government Center, and appointments are recommended.

Georgia's county property tax facts page from the state revenue department adds that failing to apply for homestead counts as a waiver, and that an application can go in any time after the home becomes your primary residence, up to April 1 of the first year you want relief. Questions go to 770.531.6720 for real property or 770.531.6749 for personal property.

sections.h2: Who owes the tax when a Hall County house sells?
sections.html:
The owner of record on January 1 is responsible for that year's bill, even if the house sells later in the year. The buyer and seller sort out who actually pays through the closing documents, and the closing attorney handles that split.

Hall County adds a step that sellers should not skip. If you sold real property during 2026, send the sales documents to the Tax Commissioner within 90 days of the due date, which works out to March 15, 2027. When the documents clearly shift liability to the new owner, the seller is no longer billed. Papers that arrive after March 15, 2027 cannot be considered. For personal property such as boats, planes or business fixtures, the January 1 owner stays liable even after a sale.

If your lender escrows taxes, the county shares the bill with the mortgage company, but the property owner is still the one responsible for making sure it is paid. Before listing, ask the Tax Commissioner for the current payoff on your parcel and bring that figure to the closing attorney. A written payoff figure from the Tax Commissioner's office keeps the closing attorney from guessing.

sections.h2: What do Hall County's numbers say about the housing market?
sections.html:
Hall County is one of the pricier counties in this part of north Georgia. The Census Bureau QuickFacts table lists a median owner-occupied home value of $350,400 for 2020 to 2024, a median household income of $80,901, and a median gross rent of $1,341.

The county grew 11.7% between the April 2020 base and mid 2025 estimate. Median selected monthly owner costs run $1,742 with a mortgage and $550 without one, and 88.3% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Hall County's 2025 permit count of 1,996 is far above the 24 recorded in Hancock County and 159 in Haralson County, a sign of where new construction is landing in this part of Georgia.

faqs.q: What is the Hall County property tax due date for 2026?
faqs.a: The 2026 bills are due December 15, 2026. They were mailed October 15, and Hall County keeps the due date at 60 days after mailing. In a typical year the statements go out September 15 and fall due November 15.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal a Hall County valuation?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date on the assessment notice. After that the value is passed to the Tax Commissioner for billing. File through qPublic, by mail to P.O. Box 2895 in Gainesville, or at 2875 Browns Bridge Road.

faqs.q: Can I pay Hall County property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes. HallCountyTax.org accepts E-Check for a flat $1.50, PayPal, and cards at 2.49% for credit and 1.50% for debit. You can also mail a check, use the Government Center drop box, or call 770.531.6950 to pay by card with an agent.

faqs.q: Who pays the tax if I sell a Hall County house in 2026?
faqs.a: The January 1, 2026 owner of record owes that year's tax, and the closing documents decide who actually pays. To move billing to the buyer, send the sales documents to the Tax Commissioner by March 15, 2027.

faqs.q: Do Hall County cities send their own tax bills?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners inside Gainesville, Flowery Branch, Buford, Braselton or Oakwood get a separate city statement in addition to the county bill. The county bill covers county and school levies only.
